entries.title: South Korea’s military service exemption could be cut for athletes
entries.summary: South Korea’s military service exemption could be cut for athletes after backlash

South Korea’s military service exemption could be cut for athletes after backlash

South Korea’s military service exemption could be cut for athletes

South Korea’s government has signalled that the current military service exemption reserved for gold-medal winning athletes could be abolished, after controversial comments made by winners at the Asian games caused public backlash.

Published On 7 Oct 2026

entries.title: German ex-spy chief arrested for treason: What we know
entries.summary: Former top spy August Hanning led the Federal Intelligence Service from 1998 to 2005.
entries.content:
Former top spy August Hanning led the Federal Intelligence Service from 1998 to 2005 and later worked at Germany’s Interior Ministry.

The man who led Germany’s intelligence agency from 1998 to 2005 has been arrested on suspicion of espionage and attempted treason, according to the country’s federal prosecutor’s office.

The office announced on Tuesday that August Hanning, 80, was arrested and faces charges including “treasonous espionage, obtaining state secrets, attempted treason” through contact with foreign intelligence services.

The office has not specified which country or countries Hanning is accused of working for.

Citing unnamed sources, however, German news outlet Der Spiegel reported that Hanning was in contact with an Azerbaijan intelligence agency representative. In 2025, prosecutors also accused Hanning of ties with Israeli spies in a separate case which ultimately led them to the ex-intelligence boss’s alleged espionage for other agencies.

If found guilty, treason carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment in Germany.

German news outlet Deutsche Welle described Hanning’s arrest as Germany’s “biggest espionage scandal of the century”.

Here’s what we know:

Who is August Hanning?

Born in Nordwalde, Westphalia, western Germany, in 1946, Hanning served as the head of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and later moved to work in the Federal Ministry of the Interior, before working as a state secretary until 2009.

He later worked as a private consultant.

German media showed pictures of Hanning being taken from his red-brick house in Norwalde, close to Munster, to a bulletproof vehicle by masked officers on Tuesday morning.

What do prosecutors allege?

They claim Hanning used classified intelligence to “draft an analysis” for a foreign intelligence service and kept “close contact” with another foreign spying service for “several years” while he was working as a private consultant.

They say that in 2010, Hanning came to an agreement to receive confidential information from his former bureau chief – who was in office until March this year and is named only as “Manfred D” – and was preparing to provide an “analysis” of it to a foreign power in exchange for money. It is unclear if the analysis was duly shared.

However, Hanning is also alleged to have passed on potentially sensitive political information, partly based on information provided by Manfred D, to a contact representing a separate foreign intelligence service.

Manfred D was also arrested on Tuesday and charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.

“Both suspects are believed to have agreed, in the spring of 2010, to have Manfred D continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the Federal Intelligence Service to Hanning in exchange for remuneration,” a statement from the prosecutor’s office said.

Over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, “many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings”, it added.

“Hanning was to capitalise on said information in the context of his private consulting services, which he had since been offering,” the prosecutor’s office said.

The alleged espionage by Hanning and Manfred D was uncovered during an investigation into a separate kidnapping case involving German businesswoman and steakhouse chain heiress, Christina Block.

In that case, Hamburg prosecutors accused Block of arranging the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Prosecutors said Hanning put Block in touch with a private Israeli espionage firm to carry out the abductions. The former spy chief and a police officer were accused of accepting more than 100,000 euros ($112,000) from Block in exchange for returning her children from Denmark, where they were living with her ex-husband. The trial is ongoing.

What do we know about the alleged documents that were passed on?

Little detail is available about the contents of the 2,000 documents, but German news outlet Suddeutsche Zeitung reported that a number of them related to Iran’s nuclear programme and the Russian military.

It added that other materials were highly sensitive and classified as secret by allied intelligence agencies in other countries.

What has the government said?

Marc Henrichmann, chairman of the parliament’s intelligence oversight committee, said in a statement to the AFP news agency that Berlin would not “tolerate the betrayal of secrets”.

“Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out,” he said, adding that Hanning’s alleged actions would amount to “trampling his official duties underfoot”.

The current head of the BND, Martin Jaeger, told the German Rheinische Post newspaper that the agency had “quickly carried out extensive internal investigations” into the former chief before federal prosecutors took over the case.

“For the BND and for me, there are no compromises when it comes to internal security,” Jaeger said, adding that it had “not called into question any of my aims or any of my priorities”.

Have there been similar spy scandals in Germany before?

Yes.

In 2023, a high-ranking German intelligence officer, identified as “Carsten L”, was charged with high treason when prosecutors alleged he had obtained classified intelligence on the war in Ukraine and the Wagner mercenary group and shared it with Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). His case is ongoing.

In 1974, West German Chancellor Willy Brandt was forced to resign following revelations that an East German spy had worked as his close aide for nearly two years.

entries.title: Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta signs new contract with Premier League champions
entries.summary: Following Arsenal's first Premier League win in 22 years, the London club has extended Mikel Arteta's contract to 2030.
entries.content:
Following Arsenal’s first Premier League win in 22 years, the London club has extended Mikel Arteta’s contract to 2030.

Mikel Arteta has signed a new contract with Premier League champions Arsenal that will keep him at the Emirates until 2030, the club announced on Wednesday.

The Spaniard’s deal had been due to expire at the end of the current season.

“It’s a privilege to commit my future to the club and to continue to work with exceptional people who want the best for Arsenal,” said Arteta, 44.

“This club is unique, its character and the way it makes you feel, and I have a great sense of privilege that our journey together will continue,” he added.

“We have already built a special bond and created memories that will last a lifetime, and what is so exciting is that this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together.”

Arteta began his Arsenal reign in December 2019 and has overseen their return to the top of English football, winning the club’s first league title in 22 years last season.

He also led the Gunners to their first Champions League final in two decades last season, but they lost to Paris Saint-Germain on penalties.

Arsenal are currently second in the Premier League, three points behind leaders Manchester City after a surprise 3-0 defeat by Brighton before the international break.

Arsenal cochairs Stan and Josh Kroenke said: “It has been an incredible journey so far and we are excited for what lies ahead in this special relationship.

“Last season was an incredible moment in Arsenal’s history, a moment in which we created memories that will last a lifetime. We’re determined to create many more in the years ahead.

“We share a special bond with Mikel. We are so proud of everything we have achieved since he returned to the club in 2019.”

Arsenal return to Premier League action with a home match against Leeds on Saturday.

entries.title: Miles away from Argentina, Messi’s farewell hits home for his Indian fans
entries.summary: Almost 15,000km away from Argentina, Messi's magical presence on the field left a lasting mark on fans across India.
entries.content:
Almost 15,000km away from Argentina, Messi’s magical presence on the field left a lasting mark on fans across India.

Messi super fan travels from India to Argentina for idol’s final game

What lengths would you go to prove your love for your sporting idol, especially when they are one of the greatest to have graced the football field?

For Lionel Messi’s superfan Yadil Iqbal, it took 40 hours of travel and thousands of dollars in expenses, all to tick off a bucket list: the once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to watch the diminutive forward’s last dance with Argentina, a game 21 years in the making.

But even as Iqbal packed his bags – carefully tucking the blue-and-white Argentina jersey and a special watch he hoped to gift Messi – there was a little twist in the story.

When he left his hometown Kodungallur in the southern Indian state of Kerala to attend Messi’s farewell friendly against Benin, the internet-popular creator did not have a ticket to Tuesday’s match at the Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires.

During the 15,000km (about 9,300 miles) journey, which involved multiple stops and long waits at airports, Iqbal documented his trip for his 1.7 million followers on Instagram. But not once did he feel anxious about the risk he was taking.

“I prayed to God that Messi wins the World Cup. Four years ago, He made it happen, and I saw it with my naked eyes,” Iqbal told Al Jazeera, referring to Messi’s first-ever World Cup victory at Qatar 2022.

“Now, nothing feels like a big challenge to me.”

Proving the saying “fortune favours the brave” right, Iqbal found the coveted match ticket hours after landing in Argentina. Getting his hands on it at the last minute in the resale market meant paying $1,000, a price he described as “three times the original value”.

But for Iqbal, who has named his toddler son “Lian Messil” – a wordplay on Lionel Messi – it is a small price to pay.

Like Iqbal, much of Kerala, as well as Kolkata in the eastern state of West Bengal, is crazy for the record eight-time Ballon d’Or winner, also the most-capped player in Argentinian history.

He may be born in Rosario, but to the thousands of supporters in those states and millions countrywide, he is one of their own.

Come any World Cup, parts of neighbourhoods in Kerala resemble a sea of sky blue-and-white – be it the Argentina flags hanging outside houses or, in some cases, the humble abode itself painted in the colours of the Albiceleste.

Iqbal, too, has a special touch of his own.

A massive mural – 32 feet in height and 20 feet in width (9.75 metres by 6 metres) – featuring Messi’s major trophies is his way of showing his love for the Inter Miami forward.

“I got that built near my house after Argentina won the 2021 Copa America, but Messi saw it on Instagram only in June this year when I wished him happy birthday,” Iqbal recalls.

“I learned Spanish from Google Translate, posted the video online and luckily, he thanked me in the comments, taking my name.”

“It was the best day of my life.”

‘He’s our idol’

In the metropolitan city of Mumbai in western India, for Sagar Shinde, who has grown up watching Messi play, the thought of seeing the greatest of all time (GOAT) wear the Argentina jersey for the last time left him in tears.

“Do you want me to cry again?” he said when asked about his emotions a day before the game.

“I am going to continue watching football, but the man who made me fall in love with the game will not be around for the team I support.”

Shinde’s love for Messi knows no bounds. He declined to choose between his engagement day and Messi’s World Cup triumph when asked to pick one as his best memory.

A tattoo on his forearm speaks volumes. It bears the date on which Messi lifted the World Cup trophy in Qatar, finally stepping out of the shadow of the late Diego Maradona.

“I challenged my friend that if Messi wins the trophy, we should get a tattoo of him. When it happened, I told him, ‘God has given us what we wanted, so we have to live up to our promise’,” Shinde, a creative producer and sports content creator, said.

Like several others, he started following La Liga club Barcelona and the Argentina national team only because of one man: Messi.

He is also the cofounder of fan club FCB Mumbai, which hosts screenings of Barcelona and Argentina matches.

Keeping up with South American football action is no joke for those living in South Asia; watching live games often demands staying up way past midnight or waking up before the crack of dawn.

But the eight-and-a-half-hour time difference was hardly a problem for the Messi and Argentina fans, with hundreds turning up for the 4:30am kickoff screening in Mumbai and beyond on Wednesday.

“Messi is unique,” Shinde said, describing the ex-Barcelona player’s talent. “If you watch football, you have to admire Messi. His elegance, dribbling skills, and the way he conducts the play … everything.

“Even when Argentina are playing badly, Messi is still good. He’s that kind of player – he can touch the ball and create magic in a second.”

“He is an idol because he motivates us so much; he never gave up.”

Why Messi means so much to football

Such is the impact of the magical Messi that his swansong drew about 85,000 fans in the Argentinian capital – more than the reported 70,000 fans who filled Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara, California, in the United States, for the 2026 Super Bowl in the National Football League (NFL).

South American football expert Martin Mazur, who is based in Buenos Aires, believes that, over the years, Messi has transformed into a “cultural icon”.

“He had been one for the younger generation [in Argentina] before winning his first trophy, but the new generation clashed with the old ones for many years, until a couple of years before the 2021 Copa America,” he said.

“In the end, Messi kind of conquered even the older generations, who witnessed five major finals lost.”

Argentinian journalist Mazur, who has written for FourFourTwo magazine and La Gazzetta dello Sport, among other leading publications, said Messi bows out from international duty, enjoying the same hero status as Maradona, who led Argentina to 1986 World Cup glory.

“What Maradona represented for the older generations, Messi now represents for the new generation,” he explained.

“For some people who weren’t born when he won, they will find out what Messi means without him in action any more, through videos, as it happened with Maradona – he had the melancholia of the people who watched him in action, but also the kind of nostalgia of people who didn’t watch him.”

London-based Argentinian journalist Marcela Mora y Araujo believes that while Messi has not changed the way football is played today, he is “one of the most influential players of his generation”.

“His individual qualities are such that he is very much unique,” said Mora y Araujo, a columnist for the Times of India newspaper. “I wouldn’t say more people play like Messi now because no one can play like Messi.

“But he has definitely marked an era, at the club level as well as the country. For Argentina, it took him a while to get the recognition, acceptance and accolade that he thoroughly deserved, but at club level, he had much more of an impact.”

Mora y Araujo, who equally spends her time between the United Kingdom and Argentina, said Argentinian fans and team alike love the “Asian love” they receive from Bangladesh, Pakistan and India.

“It is a source of enormous joy and pride for Argentinians,” she added. “There are viral videos of Indian fans chanting songs from Argentina… It’s terrific.

“I am not alone in saying that we absolutely love it.”

entries.title: Justina Shiroka Pula: Kosovo’s new president, elected during a crisis
entries.summary: An academic, former minister and a compromise choice, Pula was voted in by parliament amid protests.
entries.content:
An academic, former minister and a compromise choice, Pula was voted in by parliament amid protests.

Kosovo’s election of a new president has brought an end to heightened tensions in parliament and possibly on the streets.

On Tuesday, protests against the convictions of former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders coincided with a midnight deadline to elect a president.

Ultimately, the ruling Vetevendosje Movement (LVV) and opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK) reached an agreement on her candidacy, clearing the way for a parliamentary vote.

Lawmakers elected Justina Shiroka Pula to the country’s top office in the first minutes of Wednesday, close to the constitutional deadline, averting new early parliamentary elections that could have pushed the country into a deeper crisis.

The 81 votes she secured – one more than the two-thirds, 80-vote threshold required – were the result of a pragmatic compromise.

The parties also agreed to adopt amendments changing the legal framework governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the Hague-based court established to try former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders for alleged war crimes – an issue demonstrators had been urging politicians to address.

After a prolonged period of political deadlock, none of Kosovo’s political parties appeared willing to take responsibility for triggering another election.

“I see the election of Justina Shiroka Pula as a mix of political necessity and the need to stabilise institutions,” Donika Emini, a research fellow at the University of Graz’s Centre for Southeast European Studies, told Al Jazeera.

Kosovo had already been in a prolonged political limbo, she said, with election fatigue and increasing public dissatisfaction with the political elite.

After the Specialist Chambers verdict and 20 days of protests, including violent incidents in Pristina on the night before the presidential vote, “going into yet another election would have carried a high political cost for everyone,” Emini said.

“I see this as more than a temporary fix, but I wouldn’t read it as proof that the underlying polarisation has been resolved.

“It was, above all, a politically necessary compromise to restore institutional functioning.”

Who is Shiroka Pula, Kosovo’s third woman president?

Shiroka Pula’s election extends the run of women leading Kosovo. The 73-year-old is the country’s third female president, after Atifete Jahjaga and Vjosa Osmani.

Born in Pristina in 1953, Shiroka Pula brings to the presidency a career spanning academia, public institutions and politics.

After graduating from the University of Pristina’s economics faculty, she completed postgraduate studies in the theory and policy of economic development at the Faculty of Economics in Zagreb, then in Yugoslavia. She later earned a doctorate, researching the relationship between demographic investment and Kosovo’s economic development.

After a brief period working at the National Bank of Kosovo, Shiroka Pula began a long academic career back at the University of Pristina, rising from assistant lecturer to professor and heading the department of management and informatics.

Last December, she became the first woman to be elected head of the Kosovo Academy of Sciences and Arts, known by its Albanian acronym ASHAK.

Her path to the presidency, however, has not been solely academic.

Shiroka Pula served as Kosovo’s minister of energy and mining from 2008 to 2011. She was then a PDK member of parliament from 2011 to 2014.

That record means she should not be portrayed simply as a non-partisan academic, Emini said.

“She has a substantial political and institutional background,” Emini told Al Jazeera. “She was minister of energy and mining from 2008 to 2011 and a PDK member of the Assembly from 2011 to 2014.

“She has also had a long academic career and has worked extensively with civil society, which in Kosovo had an extensive state-building role for a long period of time,” Emini added.

The combination gives Shiroka Pula a strong understanding of Kosovo’s political and institutional landscape, as well as experience that could allow her to act as a counterbalance between institutions.

Her name was already acceptable to different political actors and was seen as less confrontational than other prospective candidates, according to Emini.

“The outcome was driven by urgency, but it also opens an opportunity to move Kosovo out of a long period of institutional paralysis,” she said.

Unlike the previous presidential arrangement, Shiroka Pula begins her term with backing from the ruling LVV and the PDK, giving her a broad political base from the outset.

But the extent of her political room for manoeuvre will depend on the relationships she develops with the Democratic League of Kosovo (LDK) and other opposition parties, as well as on the team she assembles in her office.

“The question is less whether she has that experience and more whether she will have the political courage and institutional backing to use it independently,” Emini said.

Hopes for a ‘more coordinated’ leadership

Kosovo’s president has limited formal executive powers. Yet the office carries political and diplomatic weight: The president represents the country at home and abroad, helps safeguard institutional continuity, and can mediate when relations between political parties are blocked.

Shiroka Pula’s academic, institutional and international exposure may also make her an appealing figure to Kosovo’s international partners, Emini said. But her influence will depend on how she uses the political and diplomatic space offered by the office, and on her relationship with the government.

Historically, Kosovo’s presidents have at times played a more active foreign policy role than the constitutional division of responsibilities might suggest, depending on the individual and on their relationship with the prime minister.

“I hope this presidency will bring a more coordinated foreign policy among the president, the prime minister and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs,” Emini said. “The tensions between the previous president and the government showed how costly poor inter-institutional coordination can be, including on important processes such as Kosovo’s Council of Europe membership.”

entries.title: US military aid to Israel continues three years into Gaza genocide
entries.summary: US military aid and arms transfer continue unchanged, as US public sentiment shifts.
entries.content:
US military aid and arms transfer continue unchanged, as US public sentiment shifts.

Washington, DC – Three years into Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, little has changed in terms of official US support.

The government in Washington, under former President Joe Biden and current President Donald Trump, has continued near-complete unconditional military aid to Israel since October 7, 2023, even as the region has exploded into wider conflict, including the US-Israeli war with Iran.

The US aid has persisted even through periods when the administrations offered tame criticism of the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s military offensive in Gaza, repeated violations of a “ceasefire” reached last year, and roadblocks to a more lasting peace in the Palestinian enclave and wider region.

To date, at least 74,243 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel, which killed at least 1,139 people. At least 1,460 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the October 11, 2025 ceasefire went into effect as Israel has continued to expand its area of control.

“The bottom line is that under both the Biden administration and the Trump administration, the US has continued to provide unconditional support for Israel, both in terms of finances, arms transfers and other forms, such as diplomatic support,” according to former Department of State official Josh Paul, who now runs A New Policy lobbying firm.

“That’s before we start adding in the costs of America’s wars in the region, whose causes are greatly attributable to our support for Israel and to Israel’s actions,” he said.

Military aid

The United States has for decades offered Israel outsized military support and preferential access to US weapons, with Washington providing nearly $300bn in aid since its creation in 1948 when adjusted for inflation, more than any other country.

Washington has repeatedly codified support for Israel, most notably through a 2008 law that requires the US government to assure Israel maintains a so-called Qualitative Military Edge (QME) over its neighbours.

Because of that, Israel’s military remains deeply intertwined with the US government and US-made weapons, upon which it relies for its air force, several of its most devastating munitions, tanks and other military vehicles, as well as its Iron Dome, David’s Sling and Iron Beam air defence systems.

Rights groups, including Amnesty International, have repeatedly linked US-made weapons to civilian killings in Gaza and the wider region, although Israel has blocked independent monitors from entering the Palestinian enclave.

“Because Gaza is a genocide, and the US has supplied so much weaponry, there’s really no getting out of the fact that the US has a responsibility,” William Hartung, a defence analyst who has analysed US-Israel aid, told Al Jazeera.

Since October 7, 2023, the US has provided at least $25.5bn in appropriations to Israel, money that comes directly from government coffers funded by US taxpayers.

The most direct form of US military support comes from government appropriations to Israel, which account for $3.8bn a year under a 10-year memorandum of understanding signed by the administration of former President Barack Obama in 2016.

The figure includes the $3.8bn a year appropriated in fiscal years 2024, 2025, and 2026. It also includes a towering supplemental security package of $14.1bn, passed by Congress and signed into law in April 2024.

The funding is predominantly made up of so-called Foreign Military Financing, which provides funds for US-made arms transfers and other services, and to a lesser degree, so-called offshore procurements, which provide funds for Israel to build its domestic arms industry.

Other portions of the funding are specifically allocated to replenish existing weapons stocks and maintain Israel’s air defence systems.

Israel also has access to a so-called War Reserves Stockpile, a programme that keeps a store of certain US weapons in the country, allowing for swift access upon approval from Washington.

Arms sales

Direct US government appropriations overlap with arms sales to Israel. Such sales – which must be approved by the US State Department, which in turn must notify the US Congress – can be paid for with US military aid or from other funding sources.

Nevertheless, Hartung says the vast majority of sales are paid for with US aid.

Sales can take years to deliver, depending on the availability and sophistication of the equipment being bought, entrenching the US and Israeli military in relationships long after the initial agreement.

“It’s a timeline where something approved today will do damage down the road, and the stuff doing damage now was approved some years ago,” he said.

To date, the US has approved at least $33.16bn in arms transfers to Israel since October 7, 2023, according to an Al Jazeera analysis of State Department notices to Congress.

Since the Israel military offensive began, the US State Department under both Biden and Trump has also repeatedly declared an emergency related to US national security interests when it comes to support for Israel, a rarely used legal manoeuvre that allows the administration to bypass some congressional oversight.

State Department-approved sales since October 7, 2023 have included thousands of rounds of 120mm tank munitions greenlit in December 2023 and again in August 2024, F-15 fighter jets and parts valued at $18.82bn approved in August 2024, and a $7.4bn package of bombs, guidance kits and fuses, and Hellfire missiles approved shortly after Trump took office in 2025.

At the time, Trump lifted a Biden-era pause on a pre-approved shipment of 2,000-pound (900kg) bombs to Israel.

Rights groups say the wide radius of the bombs, which can be up to a quarter mile (0.4km), causes widespread civilian devastation. A 2024 study found Israel dropped nearly 600 of 2,000-pound bombs across densely populated Gaza from October 7 to October 23, 2023.

In September, US Representative Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said he had placed a hold on a $2.8bn transfer of 40,000 2,000-pound bombs to Israel, saying he had not received assurances that the “weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with US law and with appropriate protections for civilians”.

Diplomatic cover

Beyond weapons, three years into Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, the US has also continued to offer diplomatic cover for Israel.

Before the October 11, 2025 ceasefire, that support showed up most clearly in the UN Security Council, where the US, as one of five permanent members, repeatedly vetoed resolutions calling for an end to the war.

All told, the US vetoed six separate resolutions related to Gaza, most recently in September 2025.

The US approach has since evolved into a pressure campaign against the International Criminal Court (ICC), which has issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant.

Trump initially announced plans to sanction the court and those who work with it in a February 2025 executive order. He charged the ICC had engaged in “illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel”.

The US has sanctioned a series of ICC officials, a UN rapporteur, and several Palestinian rights groups, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio promising in July to accelerate an “all of government” approach to dismantle the tribunal.

Joyce Ajlouny, general secretary of the American Friends Service Committee, has called the Trump administration’s approach “an affront to all victims and survivors of war crimes and genocide”.

Washington has taken other efforts to shield Israel from accountability.

The law appropriating the most recent round of military funding further blocks any US funding from supporting an independent commission launched by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021 investigating the occupied Palestinian territory.

It also blocks US funding for the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA).

Growing US opposition

While there has been little divergence from the executive branch in its unconditional support for Israel, the domestic political context in the US has shifted dramatically over the last three years.

A May New York Times/Siena poll found that about 68 percent of Democrats opposed providing additional economic and military support to Israel, climbing from 45 percent three years earlier. A Gallup poll from February found that while 70 percent of Republicans sympathise with Israelis over Palestinians, the share had dropped by 10 percentage points compared with just a year earlier.

Lawmakers in Congress have increasingly reflected that discontent, even if resolutions seeking to block weapons transfers continue to fall short of the two-thirds majority in the House and Senate needed to take effect.

“Years ago, even an amendment to block a sale to Israel would have been unthinkable,” analyst Hartung said. “I think the tide is turning. But I mean, the killing’s happening now, so it’s not a lot of solace unless we really can stop it.”

US Senator Bernie Sanders and lawmakers in the House have introduced legislation to block weapons sales.

A fact sheet compiled by Sanders office in 2024 pointed to the reported use of US munitions, notably 120mm tank rounds, in several high-profile killings of civilians in Gaza, including five-year-old Hind Rajab in Gaza City, as well as the use of Joint Direct Attack Munitions (JDAMS) in several high-casualty Israeli strikes.

A bill to block the sale of military bulldozers passed the Senate by a vote of 40 in April 2024, in what some advocates hailed as a historic shift.

In September, 47 Senators voted to advance a bill that would require the State Department to conduct an investigation into US citizens killed by Israel in the occupied West Bank, which could eventually lead to restrictions on military aid.

On the opposite side, pro-Israel US lawmakers have sought to formally integrate the US and Israeli military in the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for fiscal year 2027.

A version of the bill passed by the Republican-controlled House would boost technological cooperation between the US and Israel, potentially funnelling billions of dollars of US funds into Israel’s defence industry and circumventing congressional oversight.

In essence, the provision is an attempt to “transition the defence relationship from the annual appropriations cycle into the deeper machinery of the Defense Department contracting world”, according to A New Policy’s Paul, and in turn, sidestep changing public sentiment.

“[A relationship] that is less transparent, less susceptible to political pressure, and more deeply embedded in the US military-industrial complex,” he said.

entries.title: Israeli attacks across Gaza kill at least four Palestinians
entries.summary: Israeli air strike kills Palestinian Civil Defence rescue volunteer in northern Gaza.
entries.content:
Israeli air strike kills Palestinian Civil Defence rescue volunteer as he was travelling to help wounded people near Kamal Adwan Hospital in Beit Lahiya, northern Gaza, a medical source says.

Israeli attacks have killed at least four Palestinians, including a rescue worker, and wounded several others across Gaza.

The Palestinian Civil Defence rescue volunteer was killed in an air strike as he was travelling to help wounded people near Kamal Adwan Hospital in Beit Lahiya, northern Gaza, a medical source said on Wednesday.

The Civil Defence identified the victim as Mohamed Tamous.

Meanwhile, an Israeli drone strike in the southern city of Khan Younis killed Hisham Ibrahim Abu Mustafa, 60, and injured several others, Nasser Hospital said.

The body of a 17-year-old Palestinian was also brought to Nasser Hospital after he was killed in an Israeli drone strike in the Qizan Abu Rashwan area south of Khan Younis, Turkiye’s state news agency Anadolu reported, citing a medical source.

A teenage boy died from wounds sustained last month when Israeli forces opened fire east of Khan Younis, Anadolu reported, citing a medical source.

Also on Wednesday, a girl was injured by Israeli gunfire directed at displaced Palestinians’ tents in the Al-Amal neighbourhood, Anadolu reported.

Additionally, in Khan Younis, the Israeli military carried out two demolitions in the northeastern and eastern parts of the city.

The military also carried out demolitions east of Gaza City’s Tuffah neighbourhood.

Israel has killed more than 74,245 Palestinians since it launched its genocidal war on Gaza in response to the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack on Israel.

entries.title: US sets new demands for Iran deal: What are they?
entries.summary: US Vice President Vance’s call for reduced nuclear enrichment suggests room for compromise, but major obstacles remain.
entries.content:
US Vice President Vance’s call for reduced nuclear enrichment suggests room for compromise, but major obstacles remain.

United States Vice President JD Vance has called for Iran to make a “meaningful” reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity as part of an agreement to end the war, a demand experts say may signal a softening of Washington’s earlier insistence that Tehran abandon enrichment altogether.

His comments come amid hardline rhetoric from other senior US officials. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has reiterated that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, while President Donald Trump has warned the war will end through either “the nice way or the not-so-nice way”.

Officials in Tehran, meanwhile, have questioned whether Washington genuinely wants negotiations as the US-Israel war on Iran enters its eighth month.

As both sides stake out their positions, Simon Mabon, a professor of international relations at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera that the prospect of Iran seeking a nuclear weapon has remained remote. Tehran’s negotiators are more concerned with sanctions, frozen Iranian assets, the US naval blockade and fighting across the region – issues he says remain the main obstacles to a deal.

Here is what we know.

What has the US said?

Vance told the Reuters news agency that Iran needed to demonstrate its commitment to not developing nuclear weapons by changing its enrichment programme. “If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 percent enriched fuel?” he said.

“If you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue.”

Enriching uranium makes it usable as fuel for nuclear reactors or, at much higher levels, for nuclear weapons. The International Atomic Energy Agency reported that Iran had enriched uranium to 60 percent, below the roughly 90 percent considered weapons-grade. In its May 2025 assessment, it found no credible indications of a structured nuclear programme.

Vance added that the US was speaking with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, although “it’s not totally clear how their country makes decisions”.

Meanwhile, Rubio, speaking to reporters in Athens, accused Iran of missing several opportunities to reach an agreement.

“Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, simple, period, end of story,” he said.

He also claimed Iran had “lost complete control” of the Strait of Hormuz and that its economy was “in total and complete freefall”. Under “crippling” sanctions, it was “about to reach a place few countries in the world have been”, he argued.

Analysts say the comments suggest pressure on Tehran remains central to Washington’s approach, even as Vance’s wording leaves open questions about what nuclear restrictions it would accept.

What has Iran said?

Pezeshkian said on Monday that negotiations with Washington were “futile”, accusing the US of using talks while pursuing Iran’s government.

“Our problem with the United States is that every time we come to the negotiating table, war is immediately imposed upon us,” he said during a meeting with Armenia’s foreign minister.

“They have attacked us three times following talks so far; this demonstrates that they do not seek dialogue. On the contrary, their goal is to bring down the Islamic Republic of Iran,” he said, according to Iran’s official IRNA news agency.

“With an enemy that resorts daily to assassination, sanctions, pressure and threats – and breaks its promises – negotiations become futile, and our nation will not accept such an approach.”

However, Araghchi, addressing foreign ambassadors in Tehran on October 4, said, “Only negotiations based on justice and fairness” could end the conflict, suggesting there is still room for negotiations to continue and a deal to follow.

The statements follow an Iranian proposal presented during the United Nations General Assembly in New York in late September to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume negotiations. Trump subsequently rejected it.

How does this compare with previous proposals?

Iran’s latest proposal sought to build on the June 17 memorandum of understanding signed by the two countries, which briefly eased the conflict before breaking down. The new proposal, offered a few weeks ago, essentially compressed the timetable and changed the sequence of steps towards a settlement.

The proposal outlined that fighting would stop on all fronts, including Israel’s offensive in Lebanon. Washington would lift its naval blockade and oil sanctions, and release frozen Iranian assets. The Strait of Hormuz would reopen after seven days, followed by negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.

Experts say the proposal could have offered Trump a route to restoring shipping ahead of November’s US midterm elections. But differences over the sequence of events remain unresolved.

However, Mabon told Al Jazeera that Washington’s focus on enrichment risked overlooking Tehran’s priorities. “The US is trying to soften its stance on the nuclear question with the Iranians, but for the Iranians, this isn’t the real sticking point. It’s the blockade, the lifting of sanctions, the unfreezing of assets and an end to conflicts across the region.”

A deal allowing limited enrichment would also invite comparisons with the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, or JCPOA, negotiated under US President Barack Obama. The agreement restricted Iran’s nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief. Trump withdrew the US from it in 2018.

Mabon said a nuclear agreement had been possible before the current war. “Arguably, a nuclear deal was within reach at several points. We had the JCPOA, of course, but then the Iranians were at the point of agreeing something similar back in February and January. The talks mediated then all suggested a nuclear agreement could be reached, and yet, the decision was taken to go to war.”

What are the other obstacles to a deal?

Mabon said Tehran would need commitments extending beyond the nuclear question. “I think the Iranians would require the lifting of sanctions, the lifting of the blockade and the unfreezing of assets, or at least a road map to that, alongside an end to the conflict in Lebanon and a permanent ceasefire in the Gulf.”

Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains another source of uncertainty, despite Rubio’s claim that Iran has lost control of the waterway.

Although Gulf oil exports have recovered significantly, attacks on vessels continue. On Tuesday, 12 crew members on board a Panama-flagged tanker were injured by an unknown projectile while crossing the strait, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said.

Gulf oil flows, excluding Iran, reached more than 81 percent of pre-war levels in September, according to maritime intelligence firm Kpler. Wider Middle East crude exports exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days that month.

The recovery could ease pressure on the US to reach an agreement, although continuing attacks leave questions over how secure the passage is.

Mabon said Washington’s apparent softening on enrichment suggested it remained uncertain about how fully shipping through Hormuz had recovered.

“If the Americans were confident the strait was open properly, then they’d be pushing for a harder deal.”

entries.title: Girl pleads for world leaders to save her country from climate change
entries.summary: A 13-year-old girl has called on world leaders to act on climate change and save her country, Tuvalu.
entries.content:
Girl pleads for world leaders to save her country from climate change

Girl pleads for world leaders to save her country from climate change

‘We are not asking for pity, we are asking for help.’ A 13-year-old girl has called on world leaders to act on climate change and save her country, Tuvalu. Melelusi Sokotia made the plea to leaders at a summit ahead of the UN’s COP31 climate forum in Turkiye.

Published On 7 Oct 2026
